description: Yavanna is a team of six from Bath: one aerospace engineer , two chemical engineers, a mechanical engineer, a computer scientist and a physicist. We took on Dancing with the SARs, using NISAR radar to find railway slopes that are slowly moving. Our project, Kestrl, turns satellite data into an interactive 3D map that shows engineers which slopes to inspect first. We love space data, engineering and building tools people can actually use. Our team is now full.
summary:
On Britain's railways, around 150 slope failures occur every year, and most on slopes rated low-risk. In the South alone, repair and delay costs have risen by over £120m, yet some 'low-risk' slopes can go ten years between examinations. With inspection backlogs, how can engineers identify the slopes needing attention before they fail?

We're Yavanna, and we built Kestrl: a web tool that turns NISAR satellite data into actionable insights on railway slope movement, at scale.

Using NISAR data, we've divided 246 kilometres of track across six South East railway lines into 100 metre-long segments. Kestrl estimates railway slope movement, flagging segments where movement stands out from measurement noise.

On our interactive 3D map, users can can examine each segment's ground movement, terrain, geology, rainfall and signal quality. Our AI assistant takes this further, answering questions, navigating the map and highlighting relevant evidence through natural-language conversation.

We're also experimenting with machine learning to group segments by movement patterns and similarities to locations with past slope failures. As more observations and historical failure records become available, we aim to identify the patterns from those failures, helping engineers spot vulnerable slopes earlier and prioritise inspections where they matter most.

Kestrl's goal is simple: to help engineers spot railway problems before they escalate to failures.
details:
What it does

Kestrl is a screening tool for railway earthworks. It takes NISAR radar measurements of the ground and turns them into a ranked list of 100 m railway segments for an engineer to check, with a 3D map to explore them. It covers 246 km of track on six lines in South East England, split into 2,461 segments of 100 m, the segment length used in the British Geological Survey and Network Rail national earthwork hazard method.

For every segment Kestrl answers two questions. Can the satellite measure the ground here at all? And if it can, is the ground moving faster than the measurement noise allows? NISAR can measure 217 of the 246 km (88%). The rest is shown in grey, a colour reserved for “we cannot answer here”. Grey never means stable.

How it works

We used eight NISAR interferogram pairs (NASA and ISRO, GUNW provisional product, track 124 descending) covering 22 June to 20 October 2026. One pair spans a 36-day gap in the data, so nothing in the pipeline assumes even spacing between passes. The phase changes by about 400 mm across the whole radar frame because of the atmosphere, so a single reference point would be meaningless. Instead, each segment is compared with a ring of ground 400 to 1,500 m around it, which cancels most of that smooth atmospheric signal. The eight pairs are then chained into a running total, and a straight-line fit over the real dates gives each segment a speed in mm per year with its own uncertainty.

A segment is flagged only if its speed is at least 25.3 mm/yr and at least twice its own uncertainty. The 25.3 mm/yr comes from the data. It is the speed that a segment with no motion at all would exceed only 5% of the time, simulated from each segment’s own noise on the real acquisition dates. The labels are Inspect first, Inspect, Keep an eye, No clear movement and Can’t tell.

Each segment also carries the context an engineer would ask for: slope from the Copernicus DEM and, where available, 1 m Environment Agency LiDAR; rock type and man-made ground from BGS maps; seven-day rainfall from the Met Office; historical landslide records within 250 m from the BGS National Landslide Database; and radar signal quality. Every flagged segment has a plain-language explanation of why it was flagged, a movement and rainfall chart, an OS grid reference and a printable site-visit sheet.

We checked the measurements against simulated still ground. Across the Brighton Main Line the average measured speed is 10.8 mm/yr, against 8.3 ± 0.3 mm/yr for 500 simulated lines with no motion, and higher than all 500. We report that number and leave the verdict to the reader. We also cross-checked against the European Ground Motion Service. The direction of motion (towards or away from the satellite) is not yet verified, so the app shows speed only.

The app

The web app has a 3D map of all six lines on real terrain, with lenses for priority, speed, slope, rock type, man-made ground, rainfall, signal quality and landslide history. An Inspect page lists segments by priority, with a line picker, the line’s height profile and CSV export. An Evidence page shows the method, the limits and the radar granule IDs behind every number. An AI assistant answers questions using only the app’s own numbers, moves the map to what it is talking about and can read answers aloud. The whole app also runs offline as a single HTML file; without internet the assistant falls back to a built-in helper.

Experimental machine learning

We kept this separate and labelled it experimental. One model groups segments by the shape of their movement over the eight passes. Another ranks segments by how closely their slope and geology resemble places where BGS has recorded landslides. Trained on five lines and tested on the sixth, for each line in turn, the ranking does better than chance (AUC 0.605, p = 0.006) but not clearly better than slope alone. With more radar passes and Network Rail’s records of past earthwork failures, the same approach could learn what slopes looked like before they failed.

Benefits and intended impact

The Rail Accident Investigation Branch told Network Rail to use new technology such as aerial sensing, and noted that slopes rated marginal or serviceable are not necessarily reviewed by geotechnical staff. A serviceable slope can go ten years between examinations, while NISAR passes every 12 days. Kestrl gives engineers a short list of where satellite evidence justifies a site visit, and shows just as clearly where the satellite has nothing to say, so those slopes are not mistaken for safe ones. It can be extended to any line NISAR covers.

How it is creative

Where the satellite can see is a headline result, with a colour of its own. The interface is written for inspectors: plain language first, with the raw phase and coherence one click away. The assistant also flies the map to the segments it mentions, so an answer arrives as a place on the map as well as a sentence.

Factors we considered

We do not predict landslips. With eight observations a predictive model would not be honest, so the core tool is a triage layer. Radar pixels are 80 m across, so every statement is about a neighbourhood of ground, never a single structure. Speeds are annualised from four months and include seasonal clay swelling and shrinking. We also designed for accessibility: every colour has a label, motion respects reduced-motion settings, and grey only ever means missing data.

Tools

Python (NumPy, SciPy, pandas, rasterio, shapely, pyproj, h5py, scikit-learn) for the radar pipeline, statistics, geography and machine learning. HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript with deck.gl for the app, Node.js for the assistant’s server function and tests, Playwright for browser tests, Vercel for hosting, and Git and GitHub. The assistant uses the OpenAI API.
